name: Pedro Ximénez

lines.s10: Pedro Ximénez is the black, syrupy sweet Sherry of sun dried grapes: raisin, fig and coffee, poured small after dinner.
lines.s20: Pedro Ximénez is a white grape of Andalusia, dried in the sun until it is nearly a raisin. It makes a black, very sweet wine that tastes of raisin, fig and dark chocolate, for a small glass at the end of the meal.
lines.s45: Pedro Ximénez pours like syrup and tastes of raisins. It is a white grape of southern Spain, at home in the hot hills of Montilla near Córdoba, and it gives Sherry its black, sweet wine. Expect raisin, dried fig and date, then coffee, dark chocolate and liquorice. It is very sweet, thick and velvety. The grapes are laid in the sun on mats until they shrivel, and the juice is strengthened with grape spirit and aged for years in cask. Pour a small glass over vanilla ice cream, or beside blue cheese. Legend says a soldier brought it from the Rhine, but it is almost surely Andalusian.
lines.sale: Pedro Ximénez is the dessert you drink: raisin, fig and dark chocolate, thick enough to coat the glass. I would pour a small glass with the bananas Foster, or simply over a scoop of vanilla ice cream.

glass.lead: Raisin, dried fig and date with coffee, dark chocolate and liquorice, black, thick and very sweet.

ladder.where: Jerez and Sanlúcar, where the Atlantic tempers the heat

glass.structure: Very sweet. Acidity low to medium, alcohol high from fortification, body full, thick and syrupy.

home.home: Andalusia. The grape is most at home in Montilla-Moriles, in the hot hills south of Córdoba, where it also makes dry wines aged under flor, usually with no added spirit. For the sweet wine the bunches are dried in the sun on mats, pressed, fortified and aged in a solera; Jerez buys in much of its must.
home.abroad: Málaga, along the coast, also makes sweet wines from it. Beyond Andalusia it is scarce, and Argentina's Pedro Giménez, for all its name, is a different grape.

service.temp: 54 to 57 degrees Fahrenheit, 12 to 14 degrees Celsius: lightly chilled, never ice cold.
service.glass: A copita or a small white wine glass, for a pour of about 60 millilitres.
service.decant: No. It is bottled ready to pour.
service.age: Bottled ready to drink after years in cask; it keeps for years unopened and for weeks once open.

with.why: poured over the top, the wine is the sauce
salt and bite against deep sweetness
raisin and treacle meet the caramel and the rum

labels.means: The usual short name for Pedro Ximénez, on lists and labels.
A denomination near Córdoba, apart from Sherry, where the grape is most at home.
A naturally sweet wine: its sugar comes from the sun dried grapes, not from blending.
A sweetened Oloroso, often sweetened with Pedro Ximénez: softer and lighter than PX itself.
Certified average ages of twenty and thirty years in the solera.

guest.q: It looks black. Is it a red wine?
guest.a: It is a white grape. The colour comes from drying the grapes in the sun until they are nearly raisins, and then from years in cask, which turn the wine from amber to almost black.
Very: at least 212 grams of sugar a litre, and often far more. That is why I pour a small glass, as dessert itself or over vanilla ice cream.
It can be. The grape makes the sweet Sherry called PX, though much of the fruit is grown in Montilla-Moriles, a separate region near Córdoba that also bottles its own.

compare.tell: Palomino makes the dry Sherries, pale Fino to dark Oloroso, with almond or walnut; Pedro Ximénez is the sweet one, black and syrupy, with raisin and fig.
Rutherglen Muscat keeps a grapey lift of orange peel over its raisin and toffee, amber to brown; Pedro Ximénez is blacker and thicker, with fig, coffee and liquorice.

profile.st: Mahogany to opaque black · Body full and syrupy · Acid low to medium · Alcohol high, fortified · Very sweet, from sun dried grapes
profile.fruit: Raisin, dried fig, date and prune; grape syrup
profile.other: Treacle and honey; roast coffee, dark chocolate and liquorice with age; a thick, velvety texture
profile.tell: Black, syrupy and intensely sweet: raisin and fig from white grapes dried in the sun, with coffee and liquorice from long ageing in air
profile.regions: Montilla-Moriles in Córdoba, its home; Jerez, which ages wine from Montilla's must; Málaga
profile.confuse: Rutherglen Muscat keeps a grapey lift and is amber to brown; Cream Sherry is a sweetened Oloroso, lighter and less sweet; Palomino makes the dry Sherries

cards.front: Pedro Ximénez: how are the grapes treated before pressing, and why?
cards.back: They are laid on mats in the sun for a week or more, a step called asoleo, until nearly raisins. The drying concentrates the sugar for a black, syrupy sweet wine.

cards.front: Where is most Pedro Ximénez grown, and how does it reach Jerez?
cards.back: In Montilla-Moriles, a separate denomination near Córdoba, where it ripens more reliably. It is brought to Jerez as must, under a long standing permission.

cards.front: How much sugar must a Pedro Ximénez Sherry hold, and how is it served?
cards.back: At least 212 grams a litre. Serve a small pour, about 60 millilitres, lightly chilled, at 54 to 57 degrees Fahrenheit, 12 to 14 degrees Celsius.

questions.q: A guest wants a sweet Sherry to pour over vanilla ice cream: black, thick and tasting of raisin and fig. Which do you bring?
questions.exp: Pedro Ximénez is made from sun dried grapes and is black, syrupy and very sweet. Amontillado, Manzanilla and dry Oloroso are all dry Sherries made from Palomino.

questions.q: A blind wine is opaque brown black and syrupy, intensely sweet, with raisin, dried fig, date, coffee and liquorice, the warmth of added spirit and no scent of fresh grape. Which is it most likely to be?
questions.exp: Black colour, a syrupy body and raisin, fig and coffee mark Pedro Ximénez, from sun dried white grapes. Rutherglen Muscat is amber to brown and keeps the perfume of the Muscat grape.

questions.q: A guest reads that the grapes for her sweet Sherry were grown inland, not at Jerez. Which region grows much of the Pedro Ximénez that Jerez ages?
questions.exp: Much Pedro Ximénez is grown in Montilla-Moriles, in the province of Córdoba, where it ripens more reliably, and is brought to Jerez as must. The other three lie far from Andalusia.

report: Mode home, as the plan fixes it: Andalusia (Montilla-Moriles and Jerez), with Málaga and the false friend in Argentina given as abroad.

A new grape: the profile is written in the manner of GRAPES, and the two targets are Jerez and Spain, the pages whose records name the grape. Montilla-Moriles and Málaga have no page in REGIONS and are named in prose only.

No Codex record is contradicted. The Jerez record and the service reference supplied the drying on mats (asoleo), the 212 grams of sugar, the must brought from Montilla-Moriles, raisin, fig, coffee, liquorice and treacle, the pour of 60 millilitres, the ice cream and the blue cheese, Cream as a sweetened Oloroso, and VOS and VORS; the Argentina record says Pedro Giménez is not Spain's grape.

Temperature: the Codex's digestif row says about 12 degrees Celsius and its Jerez record slightly chilled; the regulatory council says 12 to 14. The entry gives 54 to 57 degrees Fahrenheit, 12 to 14 degrees Celsius, which holds both. It is warmer than the brief's row for sweet whites, on purpose.
The dry wines of Montilla-Moriles reaching their strength without added spirit stand on that denomination's own rule; the entry says usually.

The legend of the soldier who brought the vine from the Rhine is told as a legend and the soldier is not named. That the grape is almost surely Andalusian rests on The Oxford Companion to Wine and on the reference Wine Grapes, which reports a DNA study naming an old Arab table grape as its parent; the parent was left out of the entry.

The ladder is the weakest field: the grape has one climate, hot Andalusia. Jerez is set on the moderate rung only in relation to Montilla-Moriles, which is hotter and drier and where the Codex says the grape ripens more reliably; the notes of each rung speak of long ageing and of the dried fruit more than of climate. The Palomino entry sets Jerez on its warm rung against Tenerife, as the Court sets Napa moderate for one grape and warm for another.

Australia's use of the grape in fortified wines and the grape's Portuguese name were left out for want of a source read in this session. Chile's pisco grape of a similar name was left out: the Codex says only that it is not the Pedro Ximénez of Jerez in character or use.
The alias PX is the plan's. The spoken lines never use the two letters; the labels and one guest answer do.
The bananas Foster is the one dish from the Creole table.
The sources were read through search results; this session could not open the hosts directly.
